title: Same Question. Different Prompts. Different Accuracy.

intro.before: Before fine-tuning or a bigger model, change how you ask. The prompting technique decides
intro.after: , and how many calls you pay for.

bullets.text: Just a clear instruction and the input, with no examples in the prompt
Cheapest and fastest to try; the baseline for every other technique
Works well on instruction-tuned models for common, well-defined tasks
Format and labels can drift; add a schema or examples to pin them down
2–5 input → output examples show the exact pattern you want
Locks in labels, format and tone faster than longer instructions
No training: swap or add examples at any time
Longer prompts, and the order or balance of examples can bias answers
The model writes intermediate steps before the final answer
Big gains on math, logic and multi-step questions
Visible steps make wrong answers easier to debug
More tokens and latency, and a fluent chain can still be wrong
Samples several chain-of-thought answers at a temperature above 0
Takes the majority final answer: 3 of 5 votes for 53 wins
More reliable than any single chain on reasoning tasks
N samples cost N times as much; needs answers that can be compared
First prompt: break the problem into simpler subproblems
Then solve them in order, feeding each answer into the next
Generalizes to problems harder than the examples shown
Several calls, and a bad decomposition sinks the whole answer
Explores several partial solutions as branches of a tree
The model rates branches (sure, maybe, impossible) and prunes weak ones
Backtracks from dead ends, like search in puzzles and planning
Dozens of calls per problem: slow and costly, so keep it for hard tasks

principles.sub: Few-shot examples fix output shape and labels faster than longer instructions.
Ask for steps on math, logic and planning; skip it for lookups and short answers.
Self-consistency and tree search multiply calls; save them for high-value questions.

rows.q: Need a more reliable final answer
Puzzles and plans with dead ends

quote.small: Every extra call should buy accuracy.
